notes.front: What is a radio wave, in one sentence?
notes.back: An electromagnetic wave made of an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles, travelling at the speed of light.
notes.explanation: Everything a station sends travels as radio waves, so their properties explain bands and range.
notes.example: Like ripples spreading across a pond, except made of electric and magnetic fields and needing no water.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B03, T3B01, T3B04

image.alt: A radio wave travelling left to right: the electric field (solid line) oscillates vertically and the magnetic field (dashed line) oscillates at right angles to it. The wave is vertically polarized because its electric field is vertical.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T3B01–T3B03

notes.front: What is an antenna, in one sentence?
notes.back: A conductor, or set of conductors, that radiates radio energy into space when transmitting and collects it from space when receiving.
notes.explanation: It is the link between the station’s wires and the radio waves in space, so every transmitter and receiver needs one.
notes.example: The short rubber rod on a handheld radio and a wire strung between two trees are both antennas.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, pp. 1-34, 4-2

notes.front: What is the polarization of a radio wave, in one sentence?
notes.back: The orientation of its electric field.
notes.explanation: An antenna's polarization is described the same way, by the orientation of the electric field it produces.
notes.example: A wave whose electric field lies horizontally is horizontally polarized.

notes.front: What is wavelength, and how do you find it from frequency?
notes.back: The distance a wave travels in one complete cycle; in meters, about 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz. Higher frequency, shorter wavelength.
notes.explanation: Amateur bands are named by their approximate wavelength, so this link between length and frequency is used constantly.
notes.example: A 146 MHz signal has a wavelength of about 2 m (300 ÷ 146 ≈ 2.05).

image.alt: Two matched scales for wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency: 3 MHz is 100 m, 10 MHz 30 m, 28 MHz 10.7 m, 50 MHz 6 m, 146 MHz 2.05 m, 300 MHz 1 m, 440 MHz 0.68 m, 1000 MHz 0.3 m and 3000 MHz 0.1 m.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T3B05, T3B06

notes.front: What is an amateur band, in one sentence?
notes.back: A range of frequencies the rules authorize for amateurs, identified by its frequencies and by its approximate wavelength, such as the 2 m band.
notes.explanation: The rules list every band by wavelength name and frequency limits, and each licence class has its own set.
notes.example: In the US, the 2 m band runs from 144 to 148 MHz; 300 ÷ 146 is about 2 m.

notes.front: What is HF, in one sentence?
notes.back: High frequency: the range from 3 to 30 MHz.
notes.explanation: The 80, 40, 15 and 10 m amateur bands all lie in this range.
notes.example: The 10 m band (28.0–29.7 MHz) is an HF band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is VHF, in one sentence?
notes.back: Very high frequency: the range from 30 to 300 MHz.
notes.explanation: The rules' band table lists the 6 m, 2 m and 1.25 m bands under VHF.
notes.example: The 2 m band (144–148 MHz) is a VHF band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is UHF, in one sentence?
notes.back: Ultra high frequency: the range from 300 to 3000 MHz.
notes.explanation: The rules’ band table lists the 70 cm, 33 cm, 23 cm and 13 cm bands under UHF.
notes.example: The 70 cm band (420–450 MHz in the US) is a UHF band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What are microwaves, in one sentence?
notes.back: Radio waves of very short wavelength; the US Navy’s training course puts the microwave region at 1,000 to 100,000 MHz (1 to 100 GHz).
notes.explanation: The pool speaks of “UHF and microwave” signals, so read “microwave” as the frequencies above most of UHF.
notes.example: A 2.4 GHz signal has a wavelength of about 12 cm (300 ÷ 2400 m), so it is a microwave signal.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 11 (NAVEDTRA 14183), Microwave Principles, Appendix I (“Microwave region”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A02

notes.front: What is interference, as the radio rules define it?
notes.back: The effect of unwanted energy on reception: any loss of quality or information in what a receiver picks up.
notes.explanation: The unwanted energy can come from other transmitters or from other electrical sources. Many rules exist to prevent it.
notes.example: Another station starts transmitting on your frequency and you can no longer make out the station you were listening to.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: The two components of a radio wave are {{c1::the electric and magnetic fields}}.
notes.explanation: Not voltage and current, and not impedance and reactance: the wave itself is two fields.

notes.front: How are the electric and magnetic fields of a radio wave oriented to each other?
notes.back: At right angles.
notes.explanation: They travel together at the same speed, each at right angles to the other.

notes.front: Which field sets the polarization of a radio wave: the electric or the magnetic?
notes.back: The electric field.
notes.explanation: The two fields are at right angles, so naming one fixes the other; by convention the plane of polarization is the plane of the electric field.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B02, T3B01; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-10

notes.front: At what speed does a radio wave travel through free space?
notes.back: The speed of light: about 300,000,000 meters per second.
notes.explanation: This fixed speed is where the 300 in "wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency" comes from.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B04, T3B11, T3B06

notes.front: Do higher radio frequencies travel faster in free space than lower ones?
notes.back: No. All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity in free space.
notes.explanation: Microwaves, UHF and VHF all travel at the speed of light; only their wavelength differs.

notes.front: As frequency increases, what happens to wavelength?
notes.back: Wavelength gets shorter.
notes.explanation: Wavelength is 300 divided by frequency, so a bigger frequency gives a smaller result.

notes.front: Wavelength in meters equals {{c1::300 divided by the frequency in megahertz}}.
notes.explanation: 300 comes from the speed of radio waves, about 300,000,000 meters per second.

image.alt: Two matched scales for wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency: 3 MHz is 100 m, 10 MHz 30 m, 28 MHz 10.7 m, 50 MHz 6 m, 146 MHz 2.05 m, 300 MHz 1 m, 440 MHz 0.68 m, 1000 MHz 0.3 m and 3000 MHz 0.1 m.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T3B05, T3B06

notes.front: Besides frequency, what is used to identify amateur bands?
notes.back: Their approximate wavelength in meters.
notes.explanation: That is why bands have names like "2 meters" and "70 centimeters".

notes.front: What frequency range is HF?
notes.back: 3 to 30 MHz.
notes.explanation: HF sits below VHF (30–300 MHz); each range is ten times the one below.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What frequency range is VHF?
notes.back: 30 to 300 MHz.
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it, so VHF sits between HF (3–30 MHz) and UHF (300–3000 MHz).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What frequency range is UHF?
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it, so UHF (300–3000 MHz) follows VHF (30–300 MHz).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the approximate wavelength of a 50 MHz signal, and which band is it in?
notes.back: About 6 meters (300 ÷ 50): the 6 m band.
notes.explanation: The 6 m band runs from 50 to 54 MHz, so its name is the wavelength at its lower edge.

notes.front: What is the approximate wavelength of a 440 MHz signal, and which band name matches it?
notes.back: About 0.68 m, roughly 70 cm: the 70 cm band.
notes.explanation: 300 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.68 m. The US 70 cm band runs from 420 to 450 MHz.

notes.front: Is 28.400 MHz in the HF, VHF or UHF range?
notes.back: HF (3–30 MHz).
notes.explanation: 28.4 MHz is below 30 MHz, so it is HF; it is in the 10 m band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Is 146.52 MHz in the HF, VHF or UHF range?
notes.back: VHF (30–300 MHz).
notes.explanation: 146.52 MHz lies between 30 and 300 MHz; it is in the 2 m band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: Is 440 MHz in the HF, VHF or UHF range?
notes.explanation: 440 MHz is above 300 MHz; it is in the 70 cm band.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the relationship between the electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave?
notes.back: They are at right angles
notes.choices:
A) They travel at different speeds
B) They are in parallel
C) They revolve in opposite directions
D) They are at right angles
notes.choicesExplained: A: both fields travel together at the speed of light. B, C: they are neither parallel nor counter-rotating; they are perpendicular.
notes.explanation: The electric and magnetic fields of a radio wave are at right angles to each other.

notes.front: What property of a radio wave defines its polarization?
notes.back: The orientation of the electric field
notes.choices:
A) The orientation of the electric field
B) The orientation of the magnetic field
C) The ratio of the energy in the magnetic field to the energy in the electric field
D) The ratio of the velocity to the wavelength
notes.choicesExplained: B: polarization is defined by the electric field, not the magnetic field. C, D: ratios are not orientations.
notes.explanation: The two fields of a radio wave are at right angles, so one field is enough to describe the wave’s orientation; by convention the plane of polarization is the plane of the electric field.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B02, T3B01; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-10

notes.front: What are the two components of a radio wave?
notes.back: Electric and magnetic fields
notes.choices:
A) Impedance and reactance
B) Voltage and current
C) Electric and magnetic fields
D) Ionizing and non-ionizing radiation
notes.choicesExplained: A: impedance is opposition to alternating current and reactance is the opposition from coils and capacitors; neither is part of a wave. B: voltage and current describe circuits. D: these are kinds of radiation (the pool calls radio signals non-ionizing), not components of one wave.
notes.explanation: A radio wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B03, T0C01; US Navy, NEETS Module 2 (NAVEDTRA 14174), Appendix I

notes.front: What is the velocity of a radio wave traveling through free space?
notes.back: Speed of light
notes.choices:
A) Speed of light
B) Speed of sound
C) 0.86 times the speed of light
D) 1.86 times the speed of sound
notes.choicesExplained: B, D: sound is vastly slower. C: in free space radio waves travel at the full speed of light.
notes.explanation: A radio wave is an electromagnetic wave, and in free space it travels at the speed of light, about 300,000,000 meters per second.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B04; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-8

notes.front: What is the relationship between wavelength and frequency?
notes.back: Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases
notes.choices:
A) Wavelength gets longer as frequency increases
B) Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases
C) Wavelength is constant at all frequencies
D) Wavelength and frequency increase as path length increases
notes.choicesExplained: A: the opposite of the truth. C: wavelength changes with frequency. D: path length has nothing to do with it.
notes.explanation: The speed is fixed at the speed of light, so if more cycles pass each second (higher frequency), each cycle must be shorter: wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency in MHz.

notes.front: What is the formula for converting frequency to approximate wavelength in meters?
notes.back: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz
notes.choices:
A) Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz multiplied by 300
B) Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz divided by 300
C) Wavelength in meters equals frequency in megahertz divided by 300
D) Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: the formula uses 300 divided by frequency, and frequency in megahertz. C: upside down.
notes.explanation: Wavelength in meters = 300 ÷ frequency in MHz; for 146 MHz that is about 2 m.

image.alt: Two matched scales for wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency: 3 MHz is 100 m, 10 MHz 30 m, 28 MHz 10.7 m, 50 MHz 6 m, 146 MHz 2.05 m, 300 MHz 1 m, 440 MHz 0.68 m, 1000 MHz 0.3 m and 3000 MHz 0.1 m.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T3B05, T3B06

notes.front: In addition to frequency, which of the following is used to identify amateur radio bands?
notes.back: The approximate wavelength in meters
notes.choices:
A) The approximate wavelength in meters
B) Traditional letter/number designators
C) Channel numbers
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B, C: bands are not named with letter codes or channel numbers. D: only A is correct.
notes.explanation: Because wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency in MHz, every band has an approximate wavelength, and bands are named by it: 146 MHz is about 2 m, so it is in “the 2 m band”.

notes.front: What frequency range is referred to as VHF?
notes.back: 30 MHz to 300 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 30 kHz to 300 kHz
B) 30 MHz to 300 MHz
C) 300 kHz to 3000 kHz
D) 300 MHz to 3000 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A, C: these are in kilohertz, far below VHF. D: 300 to 3000 MHz is UHF.
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it: HF 3–30, VHF 30–300, UHF 300–3000 MHz, so knowing one lets you work out the others (47 CFR 97.3(b)(13)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B08; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7

notes.front: What frequency range is referred to as UHF?
notes.back: 300 to 3000 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 30 to 300 kHz
B) 30 to 300 MHz
C) 300 to 3000 kHz
D) 300 to 3000 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A, C: kilohertz ranges, far below UHF. B: 30 to 300 MHz is VHF.
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it: HF 3–30, VHF 30–300, UHF 300–3000 MHz, so UHF starts where VHF ends (47 CFR 97.3(b)(12)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B09; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7

notes.front: What frequency range is referred to as HF?
notes.back: 3 to 30 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 300 to 3000 MHz
B) 30 to 300 MHz
C) 3 to 30 MHz
D) 300 to 3000 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is UHF. B: that is VHF. D: 300 to 3000 kHz is below HF.
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it: HF 3–30, VHF 30–300, UHF 300–3000 MHz, so HF is the lowest of the three (47 CFR 97.3(b)(4)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3B10; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7

notes.front: What is the approximate velocity of a radio wave in free space?
notes.back: 300,000,000 meters per second
notes.choices:
A) 150,000,000 meters per second
B) 300,000,000 meters per second
C) 300,000,000 miles per hour
D) 150,000,000 miles per hour
notes.choicesExplained: A: half the true speed. C: the right number but the wrong unit; it is meters per second, not miles per hour. D: wrong number and wrong unit; 150,000,000 miles per hour is less than a quarter of the speed of light.
notes.explanation: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000,000 meters per second; that figure is where the 300 in “wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency in MHz” comes from.

notes.front: Which of these frequencies travels at the highest velocity in free space?
notes.back: All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity
notes.choices:
A) Microwaves
B) UHF
C) VHF
D) All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: no band is faster; frequency changes the wavelength, not the speed.
notes.explanation: In free space every radio wave travels at the speed of light. Changing the frequency changes only the wavelength (wavelength = 300 ÷ frequency in MHz), not the speed.

notes.front: How is the polarization of an antenna described?
notes.back: By the orientation of the electric field
notes.choices:
A) By the shape of the driven element
B) By the orientation of the electric field
C) By the orientation of the magnetic field
D) By the direction of radiation
notes.choicesExplained: A: the element's shape does not define polarization. C: polarization follows the electric field, not the magnetic. D: direction of radiation is a different property.
notes.explanation: An antenna's polarization, like a wave's, is the orientation of the electric field.

notes.front: Which of HF, VHF and UHF covers 30 to 300 MHz?
notes.back: VHF. HF is 3–30 MHz and UHF 300–3000 MHz.
notes.explanation: Each range is ten times the one below it: 3–30, 30–300, 300–3000 MHz.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

image.alt: A bar on a logarithmic frequency scale divided into HF (3–30 MHz), VHF (30–300 MHz) and UHF (300–3000 MHz). Technician bands are marked: 80, 40, 15 and 10 m in HF; 6 m, 2 m and 1.25 m in VHF; 70 cm, 33 cm, 23 cm and 13 cm in UHF.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 47 CFR 97.3(b) and 97.301 (eCFR as of 2026-09-22)

notes.front: A wave's magnetic field is horizontal and its electric field vertical. What is its polarization?
notes.back: Vertical: polarization follows the electric field.
notes.explanation: The magnetic field is always at right angles to the electric field; only the electric field names the polarization.

image.alt: A radio wave travelling left to right: the electric field (solid line) oscillates vertically and the magnetic field (dashed line) oscillates at right angles to it. The wave is vertically polarized because its electric field is vertical.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T3B01–T3B03

notes.front: The 2 m band and the 70 cm band: which has the higher frequency?
notes.back: The 70 cm band: shorter wavelength means higher frequency.
notes.explanation: 2 m is 144–148 MHz; 70 cm is 420–450 MHz. Wavelength and frequency move in opposite directions.
